title: Renal potassium handling: freely filtered, reabsorbed in proximal tubule/Henle, then secreted (can exceed filtered load)
vignette: A healthy 32-year-old man enrolls in a clinical study investigating potassium handling by the kidney. During the study period, he is given oral potassium supplements and potassium levels in the serum and urine are closely monitored. Compared to the amount of potassium delivered to the glomerular capillaries, the percentage of potassium remaining in this individual's tubular fluid is most likely to vary by which of the following amounts?

clues.note: A high dietary/oral potassium load stimulates the distal nephron (principal cells) to SECRETE potassium, so the excreted amount can exceed the filtered load.

clues.text: percentage of potassium remaining in this individual's tubular fluid
clues.note: Track potassium as a percentage of the filtered load along the nephron: freely filtered (100%), largely reabsorbed proximally, then secreted distally under high-K conditions.

whatMatters: Potassium is FREELY FILTERED (100% at Bowman capsule), ~65% reabsorbed in the proximal tubule (leaving ~35%), and further reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb (leaving ~10%); then, with a HIGH potassium load, principal cells SECRETE K so the amount in the collecting duct can EXCEED the filtered load (>100%). Answer A (100% / 35% / 10% / 110%).
strategy: Follow the fixed reabsorption early and the regulated secretion late. Bowman capsule = 100% (freely filtered); end of proximal tubule ~35% (65% reabsorbed); end of thick ascending limb ~10%; end of collecting duct >100% (110%) because principal cells SECRETE K on a high-K diet. Match to the option with 100/35/10/110. Reject options with the wrong proximal/Henle values (75%, 50%, 70%, 100% at Henle) - reabsorption in proximal tubule/Henle is relatively fixed.

options.text: Bowman's capsule 100%, end of proximal tubule 35%, end of thick ascending limb 10%, end of collecting duct 110%
Bowman's capsule 100%, end of proximal tubule 35%, end of thick ascending limb 70%, end of collecting duct 110%
Bowman's capsule 75%, end of proximal tubule 50%, end of thick ascending limb 25%, end of collecting duct 110%
Bowman's capsule 100%, end of proximal tubule 50%, end of thick ascending limb 100%, end of collecting duct 110%

eliminations.label: Henle 70% - too high (should be ~10%)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: 70% remaining after the thick ascending limb. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the thick ascending limb reabsorbs ~25-30% more of the filtered K (via the Na/K/2Cl cotransporter), leaving only ~5-10%, not 70%. ✅ Correct if: a segment with minimal K reabsorption.

eliminations.label: Bowman 75% - K is freely filtered (100%)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: only 75% at Bowman capsule. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: potassium is FREELY filtered, so tubular fluid at Bowman capsule equals 100% of the amount delivered to the glomerular capillaries. ✅ Correct if: a protein-bound solute not freely filtered.

eliminations.label: Henle 100% - no reabsorption (incorrect)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: 100% remaining after the thick ascending limb (and 50% at proximal tubule). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: substantial K is reabsorbed proximally (~65%) and in the loop (~25-30%), so far less than 100% remains after Henle. ✅ Correct if: a solute not reabsorbed in the proximal tubule/loop.

reasoning: Potassium is freely filtered, so 100% enters Bowman capsule
~65% is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule (leaving ~35%) and more in the thick ascending limb (leaving ~10%)
With a high potassium load, principal cells secrete K, so the collecting-duct amount exceeds the filtered load (>100%)
mechanism: POTASSIUM handling along the nephron combines FIXED early reabsorption with REGULATED distal secretion. K is FREELY FILTERED at the glomerulus, so tubular fluid at Bowman capsule contains 100% of the filtered load. The PROXIMAL TUBULE reabsorbs ~65% (leaving ~35%), and the THICK ASCENDING LIMB of Henle reabsorbs another ~25-30% via the Na/K/2Cl cotransporter (leaving ~5-10%); these segments handle K at a relatively FIXED rate regardless of intake. Potassium BALANCE is then set in the LATE DISTAL TUBULE and CORTICAL COLLECTING DUCT: PRINCIPAL CELLS SECRETE K through apical K channels, and this secretion is stimulated by a HIGH potassium load (directly and via aldosterone). Therefore, on a high-K diet, the amount of K in the collecting-duct fluid can EXCEED the originally filtered load (>100%, e.g., ~110%). (Conversely, with K depletion, alpha-intercalated cells reabsorb K and excretion can fall toward ~1%.) The correct profile is thus 100% (Bowman) -> 35% (proximal) -> 10% (Henle) -> 110% (collecting duct).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Renal > potassium handling: freely filtered (100%); ~65% reabsorbed proximal tubule; ~25-30% thick ascending limb (Na/K/2Cl); distal secretion by principal cells (aldosterone/high-K stimulated) can exceed filtered load; K depletion -> alpha-intercalated reabsorption (~1%).

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: K freely filtered, mostly reabsorbed early (fixed), secreted distally (regulated) -> can exceed 100% on high-K diet.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on freely filtered, proximal reabsorption, thick ascending limb, principal vs intercalated cells, or aldosterone? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Henle should leave ~10% (not 70-100%); Bowman = 100% (freely filtered, not 75%).

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: K freely filtered (100%) -> ~35% after PCT -> ~10% after Henle -> secreted distally (>100% on high-K diet).

firstAid.detail: Renal: filtered 100%, reabsorbed proximally/Henle, secreted distally (>100% high-K).
Renal > principal cells secrete K; alpha-intercalated reabsorb K.

memoryHook: Potassium gets fully filtered, mostly grabbed back early (fixed), then the collecting duct DECIDES - dump extra on a high-K diet, so urine K can top 100% of what was filtered.
